questions.problem:
Complete the arguments in the reasoning below to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-t}.$First, we apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
L{f(t)}=F(s)={{field-1}}
$$

We now examine the convergence of $F(s)$ for different values of $s:$

$\,$ For {{field-2}}
the integral is divergent.

$\,$ For {{field-3}}
the integral is convergent.

Evaluating our integral in the convergent case, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-1-s)t}\,\text{d}t={{field-4}}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $L{{e}^{-t}}=\frac{1}{s+1},$ 
defined for
{{field-5}}.
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st-t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-1-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-1-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-1-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne -1$ or $s=-1.$

- If $s\ne -1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-1-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-1-s}{e}^{(-1-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+1}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s+1}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>-1, \\ \infty ,\, & s<-1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(-1) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-1-(-1))t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s\le -1$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s>-1$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s>-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s+1}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s+1}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s+1},$ defined for $s>-1.$

For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{t/2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t/2}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+t/2}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/2-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/2-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/2-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne \frac{1}{2}$ or $s=\frac{1}{2}.$

- If $s\ne \frac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/2-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{1/2-s}{e}^{(1/2-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{1/2-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/2-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/2}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/2-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/2}-\frac{1}{s-1/2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/2-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/2-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>\frac{1}{2}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=\frac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{1}{2}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/2-1/2)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s\le \frac{1}{2}$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s>\frac{1}{2}$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s>\frac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-1/2}-\frac{1}{s-1/2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/2-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/2}-\frac{1}{s-1/2}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/2}$ is $F(s)=\frac{2}{2s-1},$ defined for $s>\frac{1}{2}.$

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-t/4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st-t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-1/4-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-1/4-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne -\frac{1}{4}$ or $s=-\frac{1}{4}.$

- If $s\ne -\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-1/4-s}{e}^{(-1/4-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1/4-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1/4-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+1/4}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1/4-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+1/4}-\frac{1}{s+1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1/4-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1/4-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>-\frac{1}{4}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=-\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(-\frac{1}{4}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-1/4-(-1/4))t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s\le -\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s>-\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s>-\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+1/4}-\frac{1}{s+1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-1/4-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+1/4}-\frac{1}{s+1/4}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+1/4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4s+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-t/4}$ is $F(s)=\frac{4}{4s+1},$ defined for $s>-\frac{1}{4}.$
